– million barrels a day of oilfield wastewater injected
– cataloged earthquakes of M2.5 and up since January 2015
Press play to hear each earthquake, lower and louder for larger ones. With headphones, West Texas earthquakes play in your left ear and East Texas in your right.
Data: Texas RRC UIC database; USGS and TexNet
About the data

About the data

Disposal: monthly volumes from Form H-10 in the Railroad Commission of Texas Underground Injection Control database (October 31, 2026 release), for permits to dispose into nonproductive zones (W-14) or productive zones (H-1). Enhanced recovery and storage wells are left out. Each circle is a wellbore, sized by its reported volume for the month divided by the days in the month.

Locations: wells are placed at their RRC surface locations by API number, which covers 99.8% of the disposal volume reported for 2015 to 2025.

Timeline: operators file the H-10 once a year, each permit on its own 12-month cycle, so the latest months fill in as cycles close. Wells whose filings end between August and November 2025 are drawn as gray rings at their last reported rate for the months after, up to 2,419 wells in December 2025. Most have not filed yet, though some may have stopped injecting. Statewide rates for those months count reported volumes only, so they are low. 2026 is left out.

Unusual reports: 134 well-months, at 82 wells, report more than 10 times the well's median month and over 20,000 barrels a day, which suggests filing errors. They are mapped as reported; their tooltips flag them and give the well's peak without them.

Earthquakes: events of magnitude 2.5 and up inside Texas from the USGS ComCat, which includes the TexNet catalog. Detection improved as TexNet was built out from 2017, so part of the rise in smaller events reflects better monitoring. Counting only M3.0 and up, the number still went from 21 in 2015 to 224 in 2022. Earthquakes across the state line in New Mexico and Oklahoma are not shown.

Sound: each earthquake plays once, at its date on the timeline. Pitch falls and volume rises with magnitude. Each sound is placed in stereo by longitude, so with headphones West Texas earthquakes play in your left ear and East Texas in your right.

The sound of Texas earthquakes

Texas operators injected 7.77 billion barrels of oilfield wastewater underground in 2024, up from 4.37 billion in 2015, and have reported 7.92 billion so far for 2025. Cataloged earthquakes of M2.5 and up went from 60 in 2015 to a peak of 816 in 2022.
